client: I've been struggling a lot since my partner moved abroad for work six months ago. It sounds simple when I say it out loud, but the loneliness has been really overwhelming — like I'm going through my daily life but nothing feels connected or meaningful anymore. I'm not even sure talking about it will change anything, because the situation is just... what it is, you know?
therapist: What you're describing — that hollow feeling of going through the motions without real connection — sounds genuinely exhausting, and I want you to know it makes complete sense that this has been so hard. I'm also noticing that even as you're sharing something really painful, there's a kind of quietness in how you're carrying it, almost like you've been holding this very carefully for a long time. I'm curious — when you say talking about it won't change anything, does that feel more like a belief you've arrived at, or more like a way of protecting yourself from hoping too much?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because I wasn't expecting it to land the way it did. I think... honestly, it's probably more the second thing, the protecting myself part, because I've gotten my hopes up before about things changing and it just didn't, so it felt safer to stop expecting anything. But saying that out loud makes me feel a little embarrassed, like I've just admitted I've given up without actually giving up.
therapist: There's actually something really courageous in what you just did — naming the protective layer underneath, even when it felt vulnerable to say out loud. What you're describing isn't giving up; it sounds more like a very understandable strategy your mind developed to avoid the pain of disappointment again. I'm wondering, when you imagine what it might feel like to allow yourself just a little hope about this situation, what comes up for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: When I try to imagine feeling even a little hopeful, there's this immediate tightening in my chest, like my body is bracing for impact before anything even happens. It's almost like hope itself feels dangerous, if that makes any sense. I guess part of me believes that if I let myself want this friendship to work out, I'm just setting myself up to feel even more alone when it doesn't.
therapist: It makes complete sense — your body has learned to treat hope as a warning signal rather than something safe, because hope has come with pain before. What you're describing is actually a really common pattern where our mind tries to protect us by collapsing the distance between "wanting something" and "losing something." I'm curious — when you notice that tightening in your chest, do you think it's trying to protect you from the friendship specifically, or from something even bigger, like what it would mean about you if it didn't work out?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That question kind of stopped me in my tracks, honestly. I think... it's less about the friendship itself and more about what it would confirm if it fell apart — like, that I'm just fundamentally someone people eventually leave or stop caring about. And that feels way bigger and scarier to say out loud than I expected.
therapist: What you just said takes real courage to put into words, and I want to sit with it for a moment — the fear that you might be someone people inevitably leave is such a heavy thing to carry, especially quietly and alone. I'm also noticing that even as you named something that feels so big and scary, there's a kind of stillness in how you said it, like part of you has been sitting with this fear for a long time without many places to put it. I'm wondering — where do you think that belief first took root for you, because beliefs that feel this fundamental usually have a history?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it started when my best friend in high school just... stopped talking to me one day. No fight, no explanation, just gone, and I never really understood why. I've been carrying that around for years, and I guess somewhere along the way I decided the problem must have been me.
therapist: That moment — being left without any explanation — is the kind of thing that doesn't just hurt once; it leaves a gap where understanding should be, and the mind will often fill that gap with self-blame because that at least feels like an answer. The fact that you've carried this quietly for so long, and that it's still shaping how safe you let yourself feel with people today, tells me how deep that wound actually went. I'm wondering — if your younger self had been able to hear an honest explanation from that friend, what do you imagine you would have most needed them to say?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I've been sitting with that question and... honestly, I think I just needed them to say it wasn't about something being wrong with me. Like, even if the reason was something I couldn't control or didn't make sense, I just needed to hear "this is about me, not you." But even imagining that now, I notice this part of me that thinks it wouldn't have actually fixed anything, because I'm not sure I would have believed it anyway.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — that even the reassurance you needed might not have reached you, because the belief had already taken hold so deeply that it could deflect even the truth. There's something quietly heartbreaking in that, and I notice as you're saying it there's a kind of softness and weight in how you're carrying it, like this realization is landing somewhere tender. I'm curious — if the belief that something is wrong with you isn't actually a fact but a conclusion a younger, hurt version of you reached in order to make sense of something senseless, what would it mean to start gently questioning it now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe that framing... that it was just a hurt kid trying to make sense of things. But then another part of me immediately pushes back and says, "Yeah, but what if that kid was right? What if there really is something fundamentally off about me and therapy is just going to dress it up in nicer language?" I guess questioning it feels dangerous somehow, like if I pull at that thread, I don't know what's underneath it.
therapist: The part of you that worries this is just "dressing things up in nicer language" is actually doing something important — it's keeping you honest, making sure you don't just swap one story for a more comfortable one without it being true. But I want to gently turn that same skepticism around: the belief that something is fundamentally wrong with you also came from somewhere, it was also constructed by a hurt mind trying to cope — so it deserves just as much scrutiny as any other explanation, not a free pass just because it feels more familiar. What do you think it would actually take for you to feel like questioning that belief was worth the risk?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very loud, very rapid speech

client: That's... actually a fair point, and I hate that it is, because it means I can't just dismiss what you're saying. But I think what it would take is some kind of evidence that isn't just me deciding to believe something different, because right now it feels like the "something is wrong with me" belief has a lot of proof behind it, like years of people leaving or pulling away. The risk is that if I question it and it turns out to be true anyway, I've just wasted time and made myself feel stupid for hoping otherwise.
therapist: The way you just said that — there's something urgent underneath it, like this isn't just a intellectual debate for you but something that feels genuinely high-stakes right now. And I want to honor that, because you're right that "just deciding to believe something different" isn't enough — real change needs something to hold onto. I'm wondering though, when you say the old belief has "a lot of proof," have you ever been able to examine that evidence the way you might in a court case — not to dismiss it, but to ask whether it's been interpreted through a lens that was already assuming the verdict?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... I hear what you're saying about the court case thing, and part of me gets it intellectually. But the thing is, when you've spent years collecting evidence that you're fundamentally someone people leave or get tired of, it doesn't feel like a biased interpretation — it feels like just... looking at what happened. Like, my last three close friendships all kind of faded out, and I was always the one reaching out more, and eventually I just stopped and they didn't notice.
therapist: The way you just described that — stopping reaching out and nobody noticing — that's not an abstraction, that's a real and painful thing that happened, and I don't want to gloss over how much that must have hurt. I'm also noticing something quieter underneath how you're sharing this, like you've told yourself this story so many times it's almost gone flat, as if the pain has been packed down somewhere very small. I'm wondering — when you stopped reaching out in those friendships, was there any part of you that was also hoping, maybe just a little, that someone would finally reach back first?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah... I mean, maybe. I don't really want to admit that because it sounds pathetic, like I was setting some kind of test that I knew they were going to fail. But I guess there was this tiny part of me that thought, if they actually care, they'll notice I've gone quiet.
therapist: That's not pathetic at all — that was a completely human moment of needing someone to show up for you without you having to ask, because asking can feel like it cancels out the meaning of the answer. And there's something really tender in what you just admitted, like a small, hopeful part of you was still there even when the rest of you had already braced for disappointment. I'm curious — what do you think it would feel like to let someone know directly that you need them to reach back, rather than going quiet and waiting to see if they notice?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
